prompt.brief: Design a DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-value store with partitioned storage, replication, tunable consistency, conditional writes, failure recovery, and predictable low-latency access.
successSignals: Define partition-key and sort-key access patterns, item limits, conditional writes, versioning, and consistency levels.
Use replication, quorum reads/writes, hinted handoff or repair, and membership protocols without making one node authoritative forever.
Handle hot partitions, tombstones, compaction, rebalancing, read repair, and cross-region conflict policy.
Explain durability acknowledgements, overload behavior, encryption, quotas, backups, and operational repair.

functional: Create tables and indexes, put/get/update/delete items, scan bounded partitions, and issue conditional or batch operations.
Support strong or eventual reads, TTL, optimistic versions, transactions within a defined partition scope, and backups.
Expose capacity, throttling, replica health, repair progress, hot keys, consistency errors, and request tracing.
nonFunctional: Target p99 reads and writes below 10 ms within a region at the configured consistency level.
Store billions of records by hashing partition keys, splitting hot keys, and limiting per-partition throughput.
Never acknowledge a write below its durability contract; make conditional retries and repair idempotent.
Throttle rather than overload, serve eventual reads when allowed, and preserve quorum safety during failures.
scaleAssumptions: Support 10 billion items, 1 million requests per second, and multi-region replicas with uneven tenant traffic.
Partition by application key and hash prefix; isolate hot tenants, celebrity keys, and large item collections.
Retain durable replicas, tombstones, snapshots, and repair logs while bounding caches and hinted handoff.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure DynamoDB- or Cassandra-like distributed key-valu latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
